modern:
This is the first promise God ever gave to fallen humanity. It holds the whole gospel, the very heart of the covenant of grace. Much of it has already come true. The woman’s offspring, our Lord Jesus, was bruised in his heel, and it was a terrible bruising. But how terrible the final crushing of the serpent’s head will be! In effect, that happened when Jesus took away sin, defeated death and broke Satan’s power. But it still waits to be fulfilled even more fully when our Lord comes again, and on the Day of Judgment.

For us, the promise is a prophecy that the powers of evil will trouble us in our lower nature, and so bruise our heel. But we’ll triumph in Christ, who sets his foot on the old serpent’s head. This year we may have to learn the first part of the promise the hard way, through the devil’s temptations and the unkindness of the ungodly, who are his offspring. They may bruise us so badly that we limp on a sore heel. But let’s hold tight to the second part of the verse, and we won’t lose heart. By faith, let’s be glad that we’ll still reign in Christ Jesus, the woman’s offspring.

notes.note: Humanity after Adam and Eve’s first sin ([[Gen.3.6|Genesis 3:6]]).
God’s binding promise to save his people through Christ, freely, as a gift and not a reward.
Offspring, descendants. “Her seed” points to Christ, “made of a woman” ([[Gal.4.4|Galatians 4:4]]). The “seed” of the serpent is everyone who sides with the devil.
In the King James Bible, a stronger word than today’s: to crush or wound.
In effect, in all that matters (not “almost”).
Christ’s second coming. “Advent” means a coming or arrival.
Satan, “that old serpent, called the Devil” ([[Rev.12.9|Revelation 12:9]]).

modern: This promise follows well on yesterday’s. Clearly we’re meant to become like Christ, the Head of our covenant, not only in having our heel bruised as he did, but in his victory over the evil one too. The old dragon is to be crushed even under our feet. The believers in Rome were upset by quarrels in their church, but their God was “the God of peace,” and he gave them rest in their souls. Their great enemy tripped up the careless and fooled the simple, but he would come off worst, trampled by the very people he had troubled. This victory wouldn’t come to God’s people through their own skill or strength. God himself would crush Satan. It would happen under their feet, yet the crushing would be the Lord’s work alone.

Let’s bravely trample the tempter! Not just lesser spirits, but the Prince of darkness himself has to go down before us. Trusting God without question, let’s look for a quick victory. “SHORTLY.” What a happy word! Soon we’ll put our foot on the old serpent! What a joy to crush evil! What a disgrace for Satan to have his head crushed by human feet! By faith in Jesus, let’s tread the tempter down.

notes.note: Made to match, shaped to be like. God’s people are “conformed to the image of his Son” ([[Rom.8.29|Romans 8:29]]).
Christ, who stands at the head of God’s covenant for all his people, as Adam stood for all humanity ([[Rom.5.19|Romans 5:19]]). What happened to the Head happens to his people.
Satan ([[Rev.12.9|Revelation 12:9]]).
Chief enemy.
Soon. Spurgeon lifts the word from the day’s text and shouts it.

modern: No promise belongs to just one person. It isn’t for one saint only, but for every believer. My friend, if by faith you can lie down on a promise and rest on it, it’s yours. Where Jacob “lighted,” and stayed, and rested, he took possession. As he stretched his tired body out on the ground, with stones from that place for his pillows, he hardly imagined he was becoming the owner of the land. Yet he was. In his dream he saw that wonderful ladder which, for every true believer, joins earth and heaven. And surely he had a right to the ground where the foot of the ladder stood, or he couldn’t have reached the stairway to God. All God’s promises are Yes and Amen in Christ Jesus. And since he is ours, every promise is ours, if only we’ll lie down on it in restful faith.

Come, you who are tired, use your Lord’s words as your pillows. Lie down in peace. Dream only of him. Jesus is your ladder of light. See the angels going up and down on him, between your soul and your God. And be sure that the promise is your own God-given share, and that it won’t be stealing to take it for yourself, as if it had been spoken just to you.

notes.note: An echo of [[2Pet.1.20|2 Peter 1:20]]. Here it means no promise is the private property of one person.
Came upon, stopped at. “He lighted upon a certain place” ([[Gen.28.11|Genesis 28:11]]).

Jacob’s dream at Bethel ([[Gen.28.12|Genesis 28:12]]). Jesus later said the angels would ascend and descend “upon the Son of man” ([[John.1.51|John 1:51]]), which is why Spurgeon calls Jesus the ladder.
Yes and amen: certain and settled. “All the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen” ([[2Cor.1.20|2 Corinthians 1:20]]).
A share of an inheritance.

modern: Yes, God’s people are going to have peace. The passage this gracious word comes from speaks of peace “with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground.” That means peace with earthly enemies, with mysterious evils and with small irritations! Any of these could keep us from lying down, but none of them will. The Lord will completely destroy whatever threatens his people: “I will break the bow and the sword, and the battle out of the earth.” Peace will be deep indeed when every tool of unrest has been smashed to pieces.
With this peace will come rest. “So he giveth his beloved sleep.” Fully provided for and quieted by God himself, believers lie down in calm rest.

And this rest will be safe. It’s one thing to lie down, but quite another “to lie down safely.” We’ve been brought to the promised land, the Father’s house, the room of love, close against Christ’s heart. Surely now we can “lie down safely.” It’s safer for a believer to lie down in peace than to sit up and worry.
“He maketh me to lie down in green pastures.” We never rest until the Comforter makes us lie down.

notes.note: Rest.
Birds of any kind, not only farm poultry.
Unrest, anxiety.
The chest, the place of closest embrace. The disciple Jesus loved leaned on his bosom at the Last Supper ([[John.13.23|John 13:23]]).

notes.term: “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures”

notes.note: The Holy Spirit; Jesus’ name for him in [[John.14.26|John 14:26]].

modern: When we’re called to serve or to suffer, we take stock of our strength, and we find we have less than we thought, and less than we need. But don’t let your heart sink while you have a word like this to fall back on, because it guarantees everything we could possibly need. God has unlimited strength. He can pass that strength on to us, and he promises that he will. He’ll be the food of our souls and the health of our hearts, and that’s how he’ll make us strong. There’s no telling how much power God can put into a person. When God’s strength comes, human weakness is no longer a problem.

Don’t we remember times of hard work and trial when we were given such special strength that we amazed ourselves? In danger we were calm. In grief we accepted God’s will. Under slander we kept our self-control, and in sickness we were patient. The fact is, God gives unexpected strength when unusual trials come. We rise above our feeble selves. Cowards act like heroes, foolish people are given wisdom, and the quiet ones are given what to say in the very hour they need it. My own weakness makes me shrink back, but God’s promise makes me brave. Lord, strengthen me “according to thy word.”

notes.note: All-powerful.
Losing someone close through death.
In Spurgeon’s sense, quietly accepting God’s will, not giving up.
Calm and in control of ourselves.
Act with courage.
Jesus promised that when his followers were put on trial, “it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak” ([[Matt.10.19|Matthew 10:19]]).
A prayer from [[Ps.119.28|Psalm 119:28]], “strengthen thou me according unto thy word.”

modern: Yesterday’s promise made sure of our strength for what we have to do. This one guarantees us help when we can’t manage alone. The Lord says, “I will help thee.” The strength he gives inside us is backed up by help from outside. God can raise up allies for us in our battles if he thinks it good. And even if he doesn’t send us human help, he himself will be at our side, and that’s better still. “Our August Ally” is better than armies of human helpers.

His help comes right on time: he’s always there when trouble comes. His help is wise: he knows how to give each person exactly the help that suits them. His help really works, even though human help is useless. His help is more than help, because he carries the whole burden and supplies every need. “The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man can do unto me.”

Because he has already been our help, we trust him for now and for what’s ahead. Our prayer is, “Lord, be thou my helper”; our experience is, “The Spirit also helpeth our infirmities”; our hope is, “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, whence cometh my help”; and soon our song will be, “Thou, Lord, hast holpen me.”

notes.note: Outside. “Help from without” is help from outside ourselves.
Grand, majestic, worthy of honor (not the month).
From [[Ps.46.1|Psalm 46:1]], “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”
Suitable, fitting.
Effective; actually doing what it sets out to do.

notes.term: Vain is the help of man
notes.note: From [[Ps.60.11|Psalm 60:11]]. “Vain” means useless.
[[Heb.13.6|Hebrews 13:6]].
Weaknesses ([[Rom.8.26|Romans 8:26]]).
An old form of “helped” ([[Ps.86.17|Psalm 86:17]]).

modern: This was said to a believer with childlike faith, who was ready to accept Jesus as the Son of God and the King of Israel on the strength of one convincing proof. Those who are willing to see will see. It’s because we shut our eyes that we end up so sadly blind.

We’ve already seen a lot. The Lord has shown us great things, too great to search out, and we praise his name for them. But there are greater truths in his Word, deeper experiences, higher heights of fellowship, greater works of service, and greater discoveries of power and love and wisdom. We have yet to see these, if we’re willing to believe our Lord. Inventing false teaching does terrible damage, but the ability to see the truth is a blessing. Heaven will be opened to us. The way there will be made clear to us in the Son of man. And the coming and going of angels between the higher and lower worlds will be shown to us more plainly. Let’s keep our eyes open to spiritual things and expect to see more and more. Let’s believe that our lives won’t dribble away into nothing, but that we’ll always be growing, seeing greater and still greater things, until we see the great God himself and never lose sight of him again.

notes.note: Nathanael, who believed after Jesus told him he had seen him under the fig tree ([[John.1.48-John.1.49|John 1:48–49]]).
Too great to be fully searched out. From [[Job.5.9|Job 5:9]], “Which doeth great things and unsearchable.”
An ability or power of the mind.

“Commerce” once meant any coming and going or exchange, not only trade. Jesus promised Nathanael he would see “the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” ([[John.1.51|John 1:51]]).
Dribble away, trickle off into nothing.
An old phrase for “on the increase,” always growing.

modern: Purity, and purity of heart above all, is the main thing to aim for. We need to be made clean inside through the Spirit and the Word, and then we’ll be clean outside too, by giving ourselves to God and obeying him. What we love and what we understand are closely tied together: if we love evil, we can’t understand what’s good. If the heart is dirty, the eye will be dim. How can people who love unholy things see a holy God?

What a privilege it is to see God here and now! One glimpse of him is heaven on earth! In Christ Jesus the pure in heart see the Father. We see him, his truth, his love, his purpose, his sovereignty, his faithfulness to his covenant. Yes, in Christ we see God himself. But we only grasp this as sin is kept out of the heart. Only those who aim at godliness can say, “Mine eyes are ever towards the Lord.” Moses’ longing, “I beseech thee, show me thy glory,” can only be fulfilled in us as we make ourselves pure from all sin. We shall “see him as he is”; and “every one that hath this hope in him purifieth himself.” Enjoying fellowship with him now, and hoping for the sight of God that will make us perfectly blessed, are urgent reasons to be pure in heart and life. Lord, make us pure in heart, so that we can see you!

notes.note: In older English, the heart’s loves and desires, not only fondness.
Setting yourself apart for God.
God’s nature as the God who makes promises and keeps them.
Grasped, understood.

notes.term: “Mine eyes are ever towards the Lord”

notes.note: Moses’ prayer on Mount Sinai ([[Exod.33.18|Exodus 33:18]]).
From [[1John.3.2-1John.3.3|1 John 3:2–3]]. The King James wording of the second line is “every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself.”
The sight of God in heaven that makes the soul perfectly blessed. “Beatific” means making blessed.

modern: If I want my soul to flourish, I mustn’t hoard what I have. I must share it with the poor. Being tight-fisted and stingy is the world’s way to get ahead, but it isn’t God’s way, for he says, “There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, and it tendeth to poverty.” Faith’s way of gaining is giving. I must try this again and again. And I can expect that as much prosperity as is good for me will come to me, as God’s gracious reward for a generous way of life.

Of course, I can’t be sure of getting rich. I’ll be fat, but not too fat. Great riches might make me as clumsy as very heavy people usually are. They might give me the indigestion of worldliness, and perhaps bring on a fatty degeneration of the heart. No, if I’m fat enough to be healthy, I can be well satisfied. And if the Lord gives me enough to live on, I can be completely content.

But there’s a mental and spiritual fatness I’d dearly love to have, and it comes from generous thoughts toward my God, his church and my fellow human beings. Let me not hold back, or I’ll starve my own heart. Let me be generous and open-handed, because that’s how I’ll be like my Lord. He gave himself for me: how could I grudge him anything?

notes.note: Generous, open-handed. It has nothing to do with politics here.
In the Bible, fatness means plenty and health, the opposite of being lean and starved.
Stingy, mean with money.
[[Prov.11.24|Proverbs 11:24]], the verse before the day’s text. “Meet” means fitting or right.
Very overweight.
Indigestion.
Enough money to live on comfortably.
Hold back; give too little.

modern: If I think carefully about other people, God will think about me, and one way or another he’ll repay me. Let me look after the poor, and the Lord will look after me. Let me care for little children, and the Lord will treat me as his child. Let me feed his flock, and he’ll feed me. Let me water his garden, and he’ll make my soul a watered garden. This is the Lord’s own promise. My part is to meet the condition, and then to expect him to keep his word.

I can worry about myself until I grow morbid. I can watch my own feelings until I feel nothing at all. And I can grieve over my own weakness until I’m almost too weak to grieve. It will do me far more good to become unselfish, and out of love for my Lord Jesus to start caring for the souls of the people around me. My water tank is getting very low. No fresh rain comes to fill it. What shall I do? I’ll pull out the plug and let what’s in it run out to water the wilting plants around me. And what do I see? My tank seems to fill as it flows! A hidden spring is at work. While everything sat still, the fresh spring stayed sealed up. But as what I have flows out to water others, the Lord thinks of me. Hallelujah!

notes.note: Repay, reward.
From [[Ps.41.1|Psalm 41:1]], “Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble.”
From [[Isa.58.11|Isaiah 58:11]], “thou shalt be like a watered garden.”
Let it be my part.
Gloomy; unhealthily fixed on what’s wrong.
A tank for storing rainwater.
Still, not flowing.
From [[Ps.40.17|Psalm 40:17]], “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me.”

modern: Right now there are plenty of clouds, but we aren’t afraid the world will be destroyed by a flood. We see the rainbow often enough to keep us from any fear like that. The covenant the Lord made with Noah stands firm, and we have no doubts about it. So why should we think the clouds of trouble now darkening our sky will end in our ruin? Let’s put away such groundless fears, which only dishonor God.

Faith always sees the bow of God’s covenant promise whenever our senses see the cloud of trouble. God has a bow he could shoot his arrows of destruction from. But look! It’s turned upward. It’s a bow with no arrow and no string, a bow hung up for show, no longer used for war. It’s a bow of many colors, speaking of joy and delight, not a bow blood-red with slaughter or black with anger. Let’s take heart. God never darkens our sky so much that he leaves his covenant without a witness. And even if he did, we’d trust him, because he can’t change or lie or fail in any other way to keep his covenant of peace. Until the waters cover the earth again, we’ll have no reason to doubt our God.

notes.note: The rainbow, God’s sign that he would never again destroy the earth by a flood ([[Gen.9.13|Genesis 9:13]]).
A great flood; here, Noah’s flood.
What we see and feel with our bodily senses, as opposed to faith.
Spurgeon pictures the rainbow as a war bow aimed away from the earth, toward heaven.
God’s promise of peace with his people, which he compares to his promise to Noah: “neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed” ([[Isa.54.9-Isa.54.10|Isaiah 54:9–10]]).

modern: He may put us aside for a while, but not forever. A woman may stop wearing her jewelry for a few days, but she won’t forget it or throw it on the garbage heap. It isn’t like the Lord to cast off those he loves, for “having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.” Some people talk about our being in grace and out of it, as if we were rabbits running in and out of their burrows. But it really isn’t like that. The Lord’s love is a far more serious and lasting thing than that.

He chose us from eternity, and he’ll love us through all eternity. He loved us enough to die for us, so we can be sure his love will never die. His honor is so bound up with the salvation of the believer that he can no more cast a believer off than he can throw off his own royal robes as the King of glory. No, no! The Lord Jesus, as the Head, never casts off his members. As a Husband, he never casts off his bride.

Did you think you’d been cast off? Why did you think so badly of the Lord who has promised to marry you? Throw off thoughts like that, and never let them stay in your soul again. “The Lord hath not cast away his people which he foreknew” ([[Rom.11.2|Romans 11:2]]). “He hateth putting away” ([[Mal.2.16|Malachi 2:16]]).

notes.note: Jewelry. “Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire?” ([[Jer.2.32|Jeremiah 2:32]]).
A manure heap; the rubbish pile.

notes.term: In grace and out of it
notes.note: The idea that a true believer can fall out of God’s saving favor and back in again. Spurgeon held that those God truly saves, he keeps.
Parts of a body. Christians are “members” of Christ’s body, and he is the Head ([[1Cor.12.27|1 Corinthians 12:27]]).
Promised in marriage. “I will betroth thee unto me for ever” ([[Hos.2.19|Hosea 2:19]]).
Knew and loved beforehand, from eternity.
Divorce.

modern: Has our Lord ever turned away anyone who came to him? If he has, we’d like to know about it. But there’s never been a case, and there never will be. Among the lost souls in hell there isn’t one who can say, “I went to Jesus, and he refused me.” It isn’t possible that you or I should be the first one Jesus breaks his word to. Let’s not even entertain such a dark suspicion.

Suppose we go to Jesus now about today’s troubles. Of this we can be sure: he won’t refuse to hear us or turn us away. Those of us who have often gone to him, and those who have never gone before, let’s go together, and we’ll see that he won’t shut the door of his grace in the face of a single one of us.

“This man receiveth sinners,” and he turns none away. We come to him in weakness and sin, with trembling faith, little knowledge and slender hope, but he doesn’t turn us out. We come in prayer, and broken prayer at that. We come confessing, and our confession is faulty. We come praising, and our praise falls far short of what he deserves. But still he receives us. We come sick, dirty, worn out and worthless, but he will not, in any way, cast us out. Let’s come to him again today, the One who never casts us out.

notes.note: Someone coming to Christ in faith, from the day’s text, “Him that cometh to me.”
In no way, not at all.
A hearing; the chance to speak to him, as with a king.
The Pharisees’ complaint about Jesus ([[Luke.15.2|Luke 15:2]]), which turned out to be the best news there is.
Pushes away, rejects.

modern: We who are saved find rest in Jesus. Those who aren’t saved will receive rest if they come to him, because here he promises to “give” it. Nothing is freer than a gift, so let’s gladly take what he gladly gives. You don’t buy it or borrow it. You receive it as a gift. You’re working under the whip of ambition, greed, lust or anxiety. He’ll set you free from that iron slavery and give you rest. You’re “laden,” yes, “heavy laden,” with sin, fear, worry, regret and the fear of death. But if you come to him, he’ll take your load off. He carried the crushing weight of our sin so that we’d never have to carry it again. He made himself the great Burden-bearer, so that everyone who is weighed down could stop bending under that enormous pressure.

Jesus gives rest. It’s true. Will you believe it? Will you put it to the test? Will you do it right now? Come to Jesus by dropping every other hope, by thinking about him, by believing what God says about him, and by trusting him with everything. If you come to him like this, the rest he gives you will be deep, safe, holy and everlasting. He gives a rest that grows into heaven, and he gives it today to everyone who comes to him.

notes.note: Loaded; weighed down with a heavy burden.
Greed; wanting what isn’t yours.
Painful regret for wrong done.
One who carries others’ loads. “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows” ([[Isa.53.4|Isaiah 53:4]]).
Leaving behind, giving up.

modern: Poverty is a hard thing to inherit, but those who trust in the Lord are made rich by faith. They know God hasn’t forgotten them. And though it may look as if they’ve been passed over when God hands out good things, they look forward to a time when all this will be put right. Lazarus won’t always lie among the dogs at the rich man’s gate. He’ll be repaid in Abraham’s arms.

Even now the Lord remembers his poor but precious children. “I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me,” said a believer long ago, and it really is so. The godly poor have great expectations. They expect the Lord to give them everything they need for life and godliness. They expect to see everything working for their good. They expect to have all the closer fellowship with their Lord, who had nowhere to lay his head. They expect his Second Coming, and to share its glory. This expectation can’t perish, because it’s stored up in Christ Jesus, who lives forever, and because he lives, it will live too. The poor saint sings many a song the rich sinner can’t understand. So when we’re on short rations down here, let’s think of the royal table above.

notes.note: Always.
The way God, in his providence, hands out good things. Providence is God’s care and control over everything that happens.

The beggar in Jesus’ story who lay at the rich man’s gate with the dogs licking his sores, and after death was carried to “Abraham’s bosom,” a place of comfort ([[Luke.16.20-Luke.16.22|Luke 16:20–22]]).
From [[2Pet.1.3|2 Peter 1:3]], “all things that pertain unto life and godliness.”
“All things work together for good to them that love God” ([[Rom.8.28|Romans 8:28]]).

notes.term: Not where to lay His head
notes.note: [[Matt.8.20|Matthew 8:20]].
Christ’s second coming. “Advent” means a coming or arrival.
Short rations, not enough food. “Commons” were the shared daily meals at a college table.

modern: Why don’t I call on his name? Why do I run to this neighbor and that one, when God is so near and will hear my faintest call? Why do I sit down and dream up schemes and invent plans? Why not roll myself and my burden onto the Lord right away? The runner who goes straight ahead does best, so why don’t I run straight to the living God? I’ll look for rescue anywhere else in vain, but I’ll find it with God, because here I have his royal SHALL to make it sure.

I don’t need to ask whether I’m allowed to call on him, because that word “Whosoever” is a very wide and all-embracing one. Whosoever means me, because it means anybody and everybody who calls on God. So I’ll follow where the text leads and call right now on the glorious Lord who has made such a large promise.

My case is urgent, and I can’t see how I’m to be rescued, but that’s not my business. The One who makes the promise will find ways and means of keeping it. My part is to obey his commands, not to direct his plans. I’m his servant, not his lawyer. I call on him, and he will rescue me.

notes.note: An old saying: the one who heads straight for the goal wins.
Spurgeon stresses the promise’s “shall be delivered”: not “might be,” but certainly will be.
Whoever; anyone at all.
Plans, purposes.
A lawyer who advises a client. It isn’t our job to advise God.

modern: Of course, if the Lord sent Moses on an errand, he wouldn’t let him go alone. The huge risk involved, and the great power it would take, would make it ridiculous for God to send one poor, lone Hebrew to face the mightiest king in the world and then leave him to manage by himself. It’s unthinkable that a wise God would set poor Moses against Pharaoh and the vast forces of Egypt. So he says, “Certainly I will be with thee,” as if the idea of sending him alone were out of the question.

The same rule holds good in my case too. If I go on the Lord’s errand, simply relying on his power and with my eye fixed only on his glory, it’s certain that he’ll be with me. His sending me commits him to backing me up. Isn’t that enough? What more could I want? If all the angels and archangels were with me, I might fail, but if HE is with me, I must succeed. Only let me be careful to live up to this promise. Let me not go timidly, halfheartedly, carelessly or presumptuously. What kind of person ought someone to be who has God with them! In such company I ought to be brave, and like Moses go in to Pharaoh without fear.

notes.note: Looking at one thing only. “If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” ([[Matt.6.22|Matthew 6:22]]).
Taking things for granted; acting boldly without God’s say-so.
From [[2Pet.3.11|2 Peter 3:11]], “what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness.”
It is right for, it is the duty of.
Act with courage.

modern: Our Lord Jesus didn’t die for nothing. His death was a sacrifice. He died as our substitute, because death was the penalty for our sins. And because God accepted him in our place, he has saved those for whom he made his soul a sacrifice. By dying he became like the grain of wheat that produces much fruit. There must be a long line of children for Jesus: he is “the Father of the everlasting age.” He will say, “Behold, I and the children whom thou hast given me.”

A man is honored in his sons, and Jesus has his quiver full of these arrows of the mighty. A man is represented by his children, and so is Christ by Christians. A man’s life seems to be lengthened and extended in his children, and in the same way the life of Jesus goes on in believers.

Jesus lives, because he sees his children. He fixes his eye on us, he delights in us, he recognizes us as the fruit of his soul’s labor. Let’s be glad that our Lord doesn’t miss out on enjoying the results of his terrible sacrifice, and that he’ll never stop feasting his eyes on the harvest of his death. Those eyes that once wept for us now look at us with pleasure. Yes, he looks at those who are looking to him. Our eyes meet! What a joy this is!

notes.note: Offspring, descendants: here, everyone who comes to life through Christ’s death.
Someone who takes another’s place. Christ took the punishment our sins deserved.
“Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” ([[John.12.24|John 12:24]]). “Corn” meant any grain.
A reading of [[Isa.9.6|Isaiah 9:6]], where the King James has “The everlasting Father.”
[[Heb.2.13|Hebrews 2:13]], quoting [[Isa.8.18|Isaiah 8:18]].
“As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them” ([[Ps.127.4-Ps.127.5|Psalm 127:4–5]]).
The labor of his soul, like the pains of childbirth. “He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” ([[Isa.53.11|Isaiah 53:11]]).
Terrible, awe-inspiring.

modern: There has to be confession with the mouth. Have I made it? Have I openly declared my faith in Jesus as the Savior God raised from the dead, and have I done it in God’s way? Let me answer this question honestly.

There also has to be belief with the heart. Do I sincerely believe in the risen Lord Jesus? Do I trust him as my only hope of salvation? Does this trust come from my heart? Let me answer as in God’s sight.

If I can truly say that I’ve both confessed Christ and believed in him, then I’m saved. The text doesn’t say it might be so. It’s as plain as day and as clear as the sun in the sky: “Thou shalt be saved.” As someone who believes and confesses, I can lay my hand on this promise and plead it before the Lord God right now, and all through my life, and in the hour of death, and on the day of judgment.

I’m sure to be saved from the guilt of sin, the power of sin, the punishment of sin, and in the end from sin’s very existence. God has said it: “Thou shalt be saved.” I believe it. I shall be saved; I am saved. Glory be to God forever and ever!

notes.note: Say openly, before others, that Jesus is Lord.
Declared openly.
Only.
Perfectly plain. A pikestaff was a plain wooden walking stick.
Someone who openly confesses faith in Christ.
Sin’s very existence. In heaven, sin itself will be gone.

modern: No one may turn and run on the day of battle, or refuse to go to the holy war. We have to fight if we want to reign, and we must keep up the fight until we’ve overcome every enemy, or else this promise isn’t for us, since it’s only for “him that overcometh.” We’re to overcome the false prophets who have come into the world, and all the evils that come with their teaching. We’re to overcome our own faintheartedness and our tendency to slip away from our first love. Read the whole of the Spirit’s message to the church at Ephesus.

If by grace we win the day, as we will if we truly follow our conquering Leader, then we’ll be let into the very center of the paradise of God. We’ll be allowed to pass the cherub with his flaming sword and come to that guarded tree, which if a man eats from, he will live forever. So we’ll escape the endless death that is sin’s doom, and gain the everlasting life that is the seal of innocence, the outgrowth of the undying principles of godlike holiness. Come, my heart, take courage! To run from the fight would be to lose the joys of the new and better Eden. To fight on to victory is to walk with God in Paradise.

notes.note: Overcomes, wins the victory.
The garden of God: Eden restored in heaven.
“Many false prophets are gone out into the world” ([[1John.4.1|1 John 4:1]]).
The church at Ephesus was rebuked because “thou hast left thy first love” ([[Rev.2.4|Revelation 2:4]]).

notes.term: The cherub and his flaming sword
notes.note: After Adam and Eve sinned, God placed cherubim and “a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” ([[Gen.3.24|Genesis 3:24]]).
Of which.
Take courage; pull yourself together.

modern: The ungodly world is hard to teach. Egypt doesn’t know the Lord, so it dares to set up its idols and even ventures to ask, “Who is the Lord?” Yet the Lord means to break proud hearts, whether they like it or not. When his judgments thunder over their heads, darken their skies, destroy their harvests and kill their sons, they begin to see something of the Lord’s power. Things will yet be done on the earth that bring skeptics to their knees. Let’s not be dismayed by their blasphemies. The Lord can look after his own name, and he’ll do it very effectively.

The rescue of his own people was another powerful way of making Egypt know that the God of Israel was the Lord, the living and true God. Not one Israelite died in any of the ten plagues. Not one of the chosen people drowned in the Red Sea. In the same way, the salvation of God’s chosen, and the certain glory waiting for every true believer, will make the most stubborn of God’s enemies admit that the Lord, he is God.
Oh, that his convincing power would go out by his Holy Spirit in the preaching of the gospel, until all nations bow at the name of Jesus and call him Lord!

notes.note: The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
Pharaoh’s scornful question to Moses ([[Exod.5.2|Exodus 5:2]]).
Something, a little.
Effective; actually doing what it sets out to do.
Powerful.
God’s chosen people.
Being raised to share Christ’s glory in heaven, the last step of salvation ([[Rom.8.30|Romans 8:30]]).
An echo of the people’s cry on Mount Carmel, “The LORD, he is the God” ([[1Kgs.18.39|1 Kings 18:39]]).

notes.term: Bow at the name of Jesus
notes.note: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow” ([[Phil.2.10|Philippians 2:10]]).

modern: To think about the poor, and to carry them on our hearts, is a Christian’s duty, because Jesus put them with us and near us when he said, “The poor ye have always with you.”

Many people give money to the poor in a hurry, without thinking, and many more give nothing at all. This precious promise belongs to those who “consider” the poor: who look into their situation, work out plans for their good and thoughtfully carry them out. We can do more with care than with cash, and most with both together. To those who consider the poor, the Lord promises his own consideration in times of distress. He’ll bring us out of trouble if we help others when they’re in trouble. We’ll receive very special help from his providence if the Lord sees that we try to provide for others. We’ll have times of trouble however generous we are. But if we’re charitable, we can put in a claim for a special rescue, and the Lord won’t go back on his own word and bond. Stingy old misers may help themselves, but the Lord will help thoughtful, generous believers. As you have done to others, so the Lord will do to you. Empty your pockets.

notes.note: Considers: thinks carefully about, pays attention to.

notes.term: “The poor ye have always with you”

notes.note: Remarkable, special.
Coming from God’s providence, his care and control over everything that happens.
Special, belonging particularly to us (not odd).
His promise and his signed pledge, like a binding contract.
Bad-tempered misers.

modern: If by laying his hand on it the bull became the worshiper’s sacrifice, how much more will Jesus become ours when we lay on him the hand of faith?

If a bull could be accepted for someone to make atonement for him, how much more will the Lord Jesus be our full and all-sufficient sacrifice for sin? Some people quarrel with the great truth of substitution, but for us it’s our hope, our joy, our boast, our everything. Jesus is accepted for us to make atonement for us, and we are “accepted in the Beloved.”

Dear reader, take care to lay your hand right now on the Lord’s completed sacrifice, so that by accepting it you’ll receive its benefit. If you’ve done it once, do it again. If you’ve never done it, put out your hand without a moment’s delay. Jesus is yours now if you’ll have him. Lean on him; lean hard on him; and he’s yours beyond all question. You’re reconciled to God, your sins are wiped out, and you are the Lord’s.

notes.note: An animal sacrifice burned whole on the altar. Laying a hand on its head showed it stood in the worshiper’s place ([[Lev.1.3-Lev.1.4|Leviticus 1:3–4]]).
Making peace between God and sinners by paying for sin.
From Isaac Watts’s hymn “Not All the Blood of Beasts.”
Someone sorry for their sin.
A sacrifice that turns God’s anger away by fully paying for sin ([[1John.2.2|1 John 2:2]]).
One taking another’s place: here, Christ taking the punishment due to sinners.
Welcomed by God because we’re in Christ, his beloved Son ([[Eph.1.6|Ephesians 1:6]]).
Brought back to peace and friendship with God.

modern: The way is slippery and our feet are weak, but the Lord will keep our feet. If we give ourselves up by obedient faith to be his holy ones, he himself will be our guardian. He’ll not only put his angels in charge of keeping us, but he himself will guard our steps.
He’ll keep our feet from falling, so that we don’t dirty our clothes, wound our souls and give the enemy a reason to mock God.
He’ll keep our feet from wandering, so that we don’t go down paths of error, or ways of foolishness, or the well-worn tracks of the world’s habits.
He’ll keep our feet from swelling with weariness, or blistering from the roughness and length of the road.
He’ll keep our feet from being wounded. Our shoes will be iron and brass, so that even if we tread on the edge of a sword or on deadly snakes, we won’t bleed or be poisoned.
He’ll also pull our feet out of the net. We won’t be caught by the tricks of our spiteful and crafty enemies.
With a promise like this, let’s run without getting tired, and walk without fear. He who keeps our feet will do it thoroughly.

notes.note: In the Bible, all of God’s holy people, not only the especially good.
“He shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways” ([[Ps.91.11|Psalm 91:11]]).
Steps; the way we go.
Give God’s enemies a reason to mock him, as David’s sin did ([[2Sam.12.14|2 Samuel 12:14]]).
From Moses’ blessing on Asher: “Thy shoes shall be iron and brass” ([[Deut.33.25|Deuteronomy 33:25]]).
Jesus gave his followers power “to tread on serpents and scorpions” ([[Luke.10.19|Luke 10:19]]).

notes.term: Pluck our feet out of the net
notes.note: “He shall pluck my feet out of the net” ([[Ps.25.15|Psalm 25:15]]).
Effectively; actually doing what he sets out to do.

modern: This is a true saying, drawn from the experience of a man of God, and it amounts to a promise. What the Lord has done, and is doing, he’ll go on doing as long as the world lasts. The Lord will take into his arms everyone who comes to him with a sincere confession of their sin. In fact, he is always on the lookout for anyone who is in trouble because of their wrongdoing.

Can’t we put our names to the words used here? Haven’t we sinned, sinned personally, so that we can say, “I have sinned”? Sinned on purpose, having twisted what is right? Sinned enough to find out that there’s no profit in it, only eternal loss? Then let’s go to God with this honest admission. He asks no more. We can do no less.

Let’s plead his promise in the name of Jesus. He’ll rescue us from the pit of hell that gapes wide for us. He’ll give us life and light. Why should we despair? Why should we even doubt? The Lord doesn’t mock humble souls. He means what he says. The guilty can be forgiven. Those who deserve death can receive a free pardon. Lord, we confess, and we pray you to forgive!

notes.note: Elihu, the young man who speaks to Job from [[Job.32.2|Job 32:2]] on.
Equal in effect; as good as.
Twisted, turned wrong.
The chest, the place of closest embrace.
Sign your name to; agree with.
The grave, and beyond it, hell.

modern: How this should tear up, root and branch, every silly, superstitious fear! Even if there were any truth in witchcraft and omens, they couldn’t touch the Lord’s people. Those whom God blesses, devils can’t curse.

Ungodly people, like Balaam, may cunningly plot the downfall of the Lord’s Israel, but with all their secrecy and scheming they’re doomed to fail. Their gunpowder is damp, and the edge of their sword is blunt. They gather together, but since the Lord isn’t with them, they gather in vain. We can sit still and let them weave their nets, because we won’t be caught in them. Even if they call in the help of Beelzebub and use all his snakelike cunning, it won’t do them any good. The spells won’t work, and the fortune-telling will fool them. What a blessing this is! How it calms the heart! God’s Jacobs wrestle with God, but no one will wrestle with them and win. God’s Israels have power with God and win, but no one will have power to win against them. We don’t need to fear the devil himself, or any of those secret enemies whose words are full of deceit and whose plans are too deep to see into. They can’t hurt those who trust in the living God. We defy the devil and all his armies.

notes.note: Spells and fortune-telling.
A fortune-teller hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel. Every time he opened his mouth, God made him bless them instead ([[Num.23.7-Num.23.8|Numbers 23:7–8]]).
Scheming, cunning.
“They shall surely gather together, but not by me” ([[Isa.54.15|Isaiah 54:15]]).
A name for Satan, “the prince of the devils” ([[Matt.12.24|Matthew 12:24]]).
Snakelike; cunning, like the serpent in Eden.
Be of use.
When Jacob wrestled at Peniel he was told, “as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed” ([[Gen.32.28|Genesis 32:28]]).
Armies. A Roman legion was several thousand soldiers.

modern:
When the Lord has accepted us, and we’re standing in the place of favor and peace and safety, then we’re led to repent of all our failures and missteps toward our gracious God. Repentance is so precious that we could call it a diamond of the finest quality, and it’s sweetly promised to God’s people as one of the most sanctifying results of salvation. The One who accepts repentance also gives repentance, and he doesn’t give it out of “the bitter box,” but from among those “wafers made with honey” he feeds his people on. A sense of pardon bought with blood, and of mercy we never deserved, is the best way to melt a heart of stone.

Are we feeling hard? Let’s think of covenant love, and then we’ll leave sin, grieve over sin and loathe sin. Yes, we’ll loathe ourselves for sinning against such infinite love. Let’s come to God with this promise of repentance and ask him to help us remember, and repent, and regret, and return. Oh, if only we could know the melting of holy sorrow! What a relief a flood of tears would be! Lord, strike the rock, or speak to the rock, and make the waters flow!

notes.note: Failures; things gone wrong.
Of the very best quality. Diamonds were graded by their clearness, or “water.”
Making holy.
A box of bitter medicines. Spurgeon means God doesn’t hand out repentance as a bitter dose.
The taste of manna: “like wafers made with honey” ([[Exod.16.31|Exodus 16:31]]).
“I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” ([[Ezek.36.26|Ezekiel 36:26]]).
God’s faithful love, bound by his promise to his people.
Sorrow for sin; repentance.
Moses struck the rock and water flowed for Israel ([[Exod.17.6|Exodus 17:6]]); later he was told to speak to it ([[Num.20.8|Numbers 20:8]]).

modern: Yes, we’ll come to this if we’re believers. Sorrow will end, and tears will be wiped away. This is the world of weeping, but it is passing away. There will be a new heaven and a new earth, as the first verse of this chapter says, so there’ll be nothing left to weep over in the fall and all the misery that came from it. Read the second verse, and notice how it speaks of the bride and her wedding. The Lamb’s wedding is a time of boundless pleasure, and tears would be out of place. The third verse says that God himself will live among people. Surely at his right hand there are pleasures forevermore, and tears can’t flow any longer.

What will our condition be when there’s no more sorrow or crying, and no more pain? It will be more glorious than we can yet imagine. Eyes red with weeping, stop your scalding flow, because in a little while you’ll know no more tears! No one can wipe tears away like the God of love, and he is coming to do it. “Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.” Come, Lord, and don’t delay, because for now both men and women have to weep!

notes.note: Adam and Eve’s first sin, and the ruin it brought on the whole world ([[Gen.3.6|Genesis 3:6]]).
“The holy city, new Jerusalem… prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” ([[Rev.21.2|Revelation 21:2]]).

notes.term: At His right hand there are pleasures for evermore

notes.note: Don’t delay.

modern: Salvation isn’t by the works of the law, but the blessings promised to obedience aren’t denied to God’s faithful servants. Our Lord took the curses away when he was made a curse for us, but not one clause of blessing has been canceled.

We’re to take note of the Lord’s revealed will and listen to it, paying attention not to bits of it but to “all these words.” There must be no picking and choosing, but equal respect for everything God has commanded. This is the road of blessing for the father and for his children. The Lord’s blessing is on his chosen to the third and fourth generation. If they walk uprightly before him, he’ll make everyone know that they’re a people the Lord has blessed.

No blessing can come to us or ours through dishonesty or double-dealing. The ways of fitting in with the world and of unholiness can’t bring any good to us or ours. It will go well with us when we walk well before God. If honesty doesn’t make us prosper, crookedness won’t. What gives God pleasure will bring us pleasure.

notes.note: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” ([[Gal.3.13|Galatians 3:13]]).
Canceled, done away with.
A Bible phrase for children’s children ([[Exod.20.5-Exod.20.6|Exodus 20:5–6]]). There it’s used of sin’s effects, while God’s mercy reaches “thousands of them that love me.”

notes.term: A seed which the Lord has blessed
notes.note: From [[Isa.61.9|Isaiah 61:9]], “they are the seed which the LORD hath blessed.”
Fitting in with the world’s ways. “Be not conformed to this world” ([[Rom.12.2|Romans 12:2]]).
Dishonesty, trickery.

modern: Do we need mercies for the journey? Here are choice ones: God’s presence and God’s protection. We need both of these everywhere, and we’ll have them everywhere if we go at the call of duty and not just because we feel like it. Why should we look on moving to another country as a sad necessity, when God’s will lays it on us? In every land the believer is just as much a pilgrim and a stranger, and yet in every region the Lord is the believer’s home, as he has been to his people in all generations. We may miss the protection of an earthly monarch, but when God says, “I will keep thee,” we’re in no real danger. This is a blessed passport for a traveler and a heavenly escort for an emigrant.

Jacob had never been away from his father’s house before. He had been a mother’s boy, not an adventurer like his brother. Yet he went abroad, and God went with him. He had little luggage and no servants, yet no prince ever traveled with a finer bodyguard. Even while he slept in the open field, angels watched over him and the Lord God spoke to him. If the Lord tells us to go, let’s say with our Lord Jesus, “Arise, let us go hence.”

notes.note: God’s care for us on a journey.
Someone passing through, not at home here. The patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” ([[Heb.11.13|Hebrews 11:13]]).
“Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” ([[Ps.90.1|Psalm 90:1]]).
Someone who leaves their country to settle in another. Many of Spurgeon’s readers emigrated to America, Canada or Australia.
Jacob was Rebekah’s favorite, “a plain man, dwelling in tents,” while his brother Esau was “a cunning hunter, a man of the field” ([[Gen.25.27-Gen.25.28|Genesis 25:27–28]]).
Jacob’s dream at Bethel ([[Gen.28.12-Gen.28.13|Genesis 28:12–13]]).
Jesus’ words as he set out from the upper room toward Gethsemane ([[John.14.31|John 14:31]]).

modern: Friends may be unfaithful, but the Lord won’t turn away from the soul that has his grace. On the contrary, he’ll hear all its longings. The prophet says, “Keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. A man’s enemies are the men of his own house.” This is a miserable state of affairs. But even then the Best Friend stays true, and we can tell him all our grief.

Our wisdom is to look to the Lord, not to quarrel with men or women. If our own relatives ignore our loving appeals, let’s wait on the God of our salvation, because he will hear us. He’ll hear us all the more because of the unkindness and oppression of others, and we’ll soon have reason to cry, “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy!”

Because God is the living God, he can hear. Because he is a loving God, he will hear. Because he is our covenant God, he has bound himself to hear us. If each of us can speak of him as “My God,” we can say with absolute certainty, “My God will hear me.” Come, then, bleeding heart, and let your sorrows pour themselves out to the Lord your God! I’ll kneel in secret and whisper inwardly, “My God will hear me.”

notes.note: [[Mic.7.5-Mic.7.6|Micah 7:5–6]], the verses just before the day’s text. Jesus quoted them in [[Matt.10.36|Matthew 10:36]].

notes.term: Her that lieth in thy bosom
notes.note: Your own wife; the person closest to you.
Harsh, unjust treatment.

notes.term: “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy”
notes.note: [[Mic.7.8|Micah 7:8]], which goes on, “when I fall, I shall arise.”
God as bound to his people by his own promise.
